speaker: bethmyers
text: Wait a minute until I see that we are recording on YouTube. I see now we are. So again, welcome to the First District Court of Appeals. We have one case on the docket that is going to be argued today. The other cases have been submitted. The case is Heffler versus Rempe Markets. And I see Mr. Valentin is here on behalf of Appellant. Mr. Benentendi is here on behalf of Appelese. Counsel, are you both ready to proceed this morning? Yes, I am, Your Honor.

speaker: johnbenintendi
text: Yes, Your Honor.

speaker: bethmyers
text: All right, Mr. Valentin, would you like to reserve any of your 15 minutes for rebuttal this morning?

speaker: koryveletean
text: Yes, Your Honor, I will reserve five minutes.

speaker: bethmyers
text: All right, I will keep your time. And whenever you're ready, you may begin.

speaker: koryveletean
text: Thank you, may it please the court. This case relates to a personal injury case as a result of a slip and fall incident on May the 30th, 2018 at Rempe Grocery Stores. The trial court granted summary judgment in favor of the grocery store on the defendant's motion relating to two issues. One, whether or not the store had notice of and knowledge of the hazard. And second, whether a sufficient amount of time had existed for them to discover the hazard. I believe that the trial court erred in granting summary judgment because the record evidence in this case supports that the store created the alleged hazard. As we noted in our brief, the hazard in this particular case is water that had accumulated on the ground near the freezer doors of a particular aisle. The appellant and her fiance at the time were shopping, proceeding down the aisle. She was positioned on the right hand side of the aisle way closest to the freezer doors, which would have been directly to her right. And she slipped and fell on water, a puddle of water that the record establishes is somewhere between 12 to 16 inches in diameter. As a result of her fall, she was injured. The store manager in this particular case, Thomas Moore is of importance because he testified in his deposition that after the incident, he was proceeding towards a set of double doors going back to the stock room. And he turned and noticed to his right on the ground, this puddle of water. And he discovered this hazard prior to receiving the intercom call to report to customer service to meet the appellant. The store manager, Mr. Moore cleaned up the water and later described in an incident report, as well as in his record deposition testimony that he inspected the area, confirmed that it was water, identified a trail of water that was coming from the freezers and identified three door seals on the particular freezer doors that were defective, allowing the water to leak from the freezer doors onto the floor and accumulate in this 12 inch to 16 inch diameter puddle in the walkway. Normally, as your honor knows, and the court's well aware, the first obstacle in these slip and fall cases is to identify the hazard. And in most of these cases nowadays, that can be a fatal issue because a lot of injured claimants cannot identify the source. Well, in this particular case, we have identified the source. The store manager himself has identified the source and also identified the cause of allowing the water to accumulate and leak from the freezer onto the ground. And that's the three defective door seals. We believe the lower court erred in granting summary judgment because Ohio case law is very clear that when a dangerous condition is created by the property owner or occupant, that notice is not required and that they have actual knowledge of the condition that they created.

speaker: gingerbock
text: Council, couldn't it have been a customer who caused- No, ma'am.

speaker: koryveletean
text: No, ma'am. The store manager was very clear in his deposition testimony that this is water, there was a trail of water leading from the freezers.

speaker: gingerbock
text: I understand that, but as far as the freezer doors themselves, could it have been a customer that caused that, caused the seals to become damaged?

speaker: koryveletean
text: I don't believe so. I think the record is very clear and rebuts any reasonable, I believe that to be an unreasonable conclusion with all due respect, your honor. I think that was completely contrary to the record evidence. In this particular case, when you have knowledge of the condition, then the necessary element of a negligence claim or a cause of action is met. If you cannot prove actual knowledge, and we argued in the alternative that constructive knowledge supports an issue of fact that would preclude the lower court from granting sodomy judgment. In this particular case, if you cannot establish actual knowledge, then evidence, the record evidence, if it shows the length of time during which the hazard existed is necessary and can support an inference that the owner had constructive knowledge. And physical evidence is sufficient to create an issue of fact as to whether the store had constructive knowledge of the water puddle in this case. In particular, the record evidence supports the following physical evidence. There was the size of a puddle. It was 12 to 16 inches in diameter. There was a leak coming from the freezer itself. It was not actively leaking at the time, according to the store manager, but he did see the trail of water coming from there. So you also have the issue with the discoloration on the door. Now, whether or not it's rust, whether or not it's discoloration, I believe that that is a issue of fact that any reasonable juror can make based on their own experience, knowing that discoloration relating to rust does not occur immediately. And it suggests that there is an issue that has been present for an extended period of time in that particular case. The fact that there were issues with other freezers, the record evidence supports that in this particular case, there was a humidity issue relating to another freezer, okay? And bring to the court's attention two cases, the Jordan versus Simon property. It's 205 Ohio 4480. And then you have the state of morale versus the Meijer stores which is 2016 Ohio 1432. And those two cases are very important because in the Jordan case particularly, you dealt with a skylight that had leaked and it was a different skylight that leaked that caused the injury to Jordan in that case. But the court concluded that it was the defendant that was in the better position to prevent hazards, to invitees and the fact that they knew that there were skylights that had existed in the past creates a reasonable risk that a skylight could leak in the future. Well, in this case, you had freezer doors that had a water condensation issue. That is where the water was coming from. That's the cause of the water, causing it to accumulate inside the freezer, but it's the defective door seals that allows the water to go from inside the freezer out into the walkway, injuring invitees.

speaker: gingerbock
text: Council, in the defendant's brief, that police brief, he brought up that the reports, the maintenance reports that talked about the other area had not been properly authenticated. Can you speak to that please?

speaker: koryveletean
text: I don't think it's an issue, a relative relevant issue as it relates to both the summary judgment and the appeal. Now, I believe that that is a total red herring because you still have the record evidence from the store manager relating to and discussing the other instances, the other freezers, okay? He testified about that. But then also, if you look at the testimony closely, you're gonna see that Mr. Benatendi himself goes as far as to reference the specific reports that he provided during discovery. He identifies me personally. So if you go back and you look at that particular section of the store manager's deposition, you're gonna see that Mr. Benatendi himself acknowledged that the forms that the deponent was referencing was in fact the same forms that they produced in the discovery. I think the testimony in and of itself supports an issue of fact relating to constructive knowledge without getting into the authentication issue that may be relevant more for trial purposes. Also, the discoverability, I believe, is gonna be an important issue relating to constructive knowledge because in this particular case, you have the store manager who was walking towards the back storage door, okay? And he identified all the different people that were working at the store at the time of the incident. He identified all the particular people that had been working in this particular department. He described the job duties that the employees had that worked in this particular department. He described how they, on a regular basis, go up and down the aisleway checking to make sure that the freezers, whether or not they need to be stocked of different products at the time. There's nothing that he did unusual. There's nothing that he did extraordinary. There's nothing that he did that any other employee that was working at the Remke store that day could have and should have done. And that's basically exercise ordinary reasonable care in performing their legal duty to perform inspections. Okay, there's nothing that this employee did. He didn't disassemble the doors. He didn't go over and disassemble the freezers. He didn't open it up and try to figure out where the water was coming from. He determined that based on ordinary exercise of a reasonable care, just a visual inspection determined that.

speaker: bethmyers
text: Mr. Valentin, you are at your time. If you would like to reserve five minutes, I'll let you wrap it up.

speaker: koryveletean
text: No, Your Honor, I'll go ahead and conclude my initial portion at this time.

speaker: bethmyers
text: All right, thank you. Mr. Benatendi, you have 15 minutes.

speaker: johnbenintendi
text: Thank you, Your Honor. I think what I'd like to do first is to address the two questions that were asked by Judge Bach. First of all, yes, we don't have any evidence in this case as to why the seals were defective. It could have been a customer. It could have been time. It could have been something else. The point is we don't know, and there's no evidence to it. So we don't know how long they have been defective. There's no evidence whatsoever to that issue. This is why the trial court granted summary judgment. She basically said, this is mere speculation. If we let the jury decide these issues, they're just speculating as to what it might be based upon the evidence in the record. And that's a key issue here. It's not what evidence do we have, it's the evidence that we don't have that's key to this case. And the other question was brought up about the authenticity. Appellant is claiming my own statements, but if you look closely at my brief, I did argue at the lower court that the maintenance records were not properly authenticated and should not be considered by the trial court. But then I did say in the event that the trial court does consider them, they're still not dispositive of this issue. And summary judgment still was properly granted. That's what I said. So I didn't make a formal motion to exclude, I just argued that, hey, they haven't been authenticated. And I cited rule 56 that clearly indicates what evidence is proper and what's not. And since no questions were asked of Mr. Moore whatsoever regarding these maintenance logs during his deposition, they were not properly authenticated. Documents are not authenticated merely by production during the discovery phase of a case. You either have to have sworn testimony as to their authenticity through deposition or affidavit. So you still have to do that. It was not done here. So they should not have been considered by the court and they shouldn't be considered by this court in the event that this court decides, should we or should we not look at those maintenance reports since this is a de novo review on summary judgment. So the issue then is, well, what if you do look at the maintenance reports, which is why I had to go out and I did file an affidavit of Thomas Moore regarding those maintenance logs because they were attached to the memorandum in opposition to the motion for summary judgment without being authenticated. But again, it was, well, what if the court does consider them? That is where the affidavit comes in, where Mr. Moore says, it wasn't this freezer, there have been no evidence of prior problems in aisle 23. And that's where this file occurred. Now, were there other open freezers in other areas of the store that they had a humidity issue? Yes, he admits that in the maintenance log to the extent that it's considered, but it's not the type of freezer of which involves this fall. It's a different type of freezer. So it's also not in the same area. So it was important that in my reply to the summary judgment that I clarified those issues in the event that the maintenance logs were considered. And so that's why that was done, but they should not be considered. And that was an issue at the trial court level. Now, as to the puddle, we don't know how long the water was there. In all the argument that we heard this morning, not once did you hear how long the water was there,

speaker: gingerbock
text: not once. Counsel, how would you distinguish this case from the Youngerman versus Meyer case?

speaker: johnbenintendi
text: Okay, the Youngerman case dealt with evidence that allows an inference from the physical appearance, character, or nature of the substance on the floor. So in effect, in the Fields case, there was dried yogurt, but it was crusty, it was dried out, and there can be an inference that it was there for a long enough period of time because of those characteristics. In this particular case, we have a puddle of water. There was no evidence whatsoever as to was it cold still, was it lukewarm still, or was it? Because if it came out of a freezer, there could be an inference that it was cold water. She never testified it was lukewarm. If she would have said it was lukewarm, then there would have been some inference that may have been able to be concluded that the water was there for a period of time that allowed it to warm from the freezer temperature. That's not here.

speaker: bethmyers
text: Couldn't because of the quantity of the water, couldn't an inference been made that if it was leaking and dripping from the defective seal that that had to have occurred over time and not in a short period of time?

speaker: johnbenintendi
text: If there was any evidence as to how the water was exiting the cooler, maybe, but there's none here.

speaker: bethmyers
text: I don't think- Wasn't there testimony that there was a trail of water from the freezer to the floor? And isn't that an inference that a trier of fact should be able to consider as to whether there was constructive notice?

speaker: johnbenintendi
text: No, because there was, Mr. Moore testified there was a trail leading from the bottom of the freezer to the puddle. Now, the only evidence about the seals was from Thomas Moore who said, I looked at him after the fall, but there was no evidence that I know of that where Mr. Moore said I saw it dripping or whatnot. So we have no idea as to the speed that this puddle formed. We just don't know. And that's the whole issue in this case is what do we not know? And we don't know, did it take a minute? Did it take five minutes? Did it take 30 seconds? We just have no idea. We don't actually know how much water there was. We know the diameter, but do we know the depth? We don't. Do we know the temperature? We don't. And getting back to the Ungerman case, there was no evidence that the water was dirty as if other people had walked through it. We don't have any evidence that the water was spread so that other people had walked through it or pushed their cart through it. So that's what distinguishes this case from the Ungerman case. There was no evidence as to the physical characteristics of the puddle other than here's the diameter and that's it.

speaker: robertwinkler
text: Let me, Mr. Benatendi, it sounds like once the manager mopped up the water that resolved the issues, is that correct? In other words, the freezer stopped leaking.

speaker: johnbenintendi
text: Well, I don't know if that is correct because there may have been leaks after the plaintiff fell. And the reason being is that the store closed within months of this fall. It was closing anyway. So the freezers were gone. But the point here is that even if there were leaks after, then one, there would be knowledge, but that's not what we have here. Two is they could have placed cones and warning signs, which is required if they have knowledge of a hazardous condition. But we don't have any evidence provided by the plaintiff or the appellant in this case that the store had actual notice that there were issues with this particular freezer or freezers in aisle 23 prior to this incident. And in fact, the plaintiff herself said she goes there two or three times a week or did when the store was open and never had an issue whatsoever. Mr. Gibson testified to the same thing. They've never had a problem at that store before, never even known of a problem at this store before. So it really comes down to the notice element. And I believe that's what the trial court ultimately decided was that there was no notice on part of the store for this particular hazard at the time that the plaintiff slipped. We didn't create it. That's what differentiates the Jordan and the Morrell because in the Jordan case, the problem was there were leaks from lights, same lights, maybe same installer, and there were documentation, there were logs by the landowner of these prior issues. There are none here. They were the same type of skylight. These are all different freezers. So there's distinguishing characteristics between our case and the Jordan case. Now, appellant also brought up the case of the estate of Morrell. That case involved Meyer where they would put pallets of jugs of water on wooden pallets that they knew had nails and had punctured these jugs of water before. There was also testimony from a prior employee in that case that adduced evidence that suggests Meyer did know about this issue. It was an ongoing issue, but they still use the same pallets with the same problems and the nails, et cetera. So there was prior knowledge again of the same condition. We don't have that here. We have no evidence whatsoever of any prior issues here. So that's what distinguishes those two cases. The Tandy case and the Lauderbeck case was two cases that appellant cites, but the issue there is that employees of the stores actively engaged in negligent conduct that caused the hazard. One was placing a doormat improperly, and the other was the employee was actually mopping the same area where the plaintiff fell. So they didn't have to prove actual knowledge because the employees actually placed or mopped improperly. So they're deemed to have knowledge. That makes sense. Here, no employee engaged in any active conduct that caused the water to be on the floor. So those two cases don't apply. So you have to either show then actual or constructive knowledge. Actual knowledge is somebody told us or we have seen it before. No evidence of that. So now we get to the last notice, which is constructive. And the Supreme Court has said in Presley versus Norwood that the plaintiff must show that the danger or hazard existed for a sufficient amount of time that the failure to warn against it or to remove it was a breach of ordinary care. So that's why the time-

speaker: bethmyers
text: They can do that by inference, correct? Back to some of the case law. If the yogurt is crusty, there's an inference it's been there for a while. That's true. What you earlier was by the quantity of the water, can it be inferred it was there for a while?

speaker: johnbenintendi
text: Well, again, all we know is the diameter. Now, whether that might be a 16th of an inch deep, eighth of an inch deep, just a very thin amount of, we don't know the amount of water. That's the point. We just know one aspect of it. That's it. But it takes more than that. In the Youngerman case and in the Fields case, there were different aspects that did allow a reasonable inference. We don't have that here. We don't know timing. We don't know amount other than diameter. There's nothing that indicates other people had walked through it or that it was dirty or that it was warm. We don't know. And it's not the appellant's burden to demonstrate those. It's the plaintiff's burden to prove it. And so it's the lack of evidence that's key here. We can think in our minds it would drip slowly. We can do that. But it must be based on some evidence that is presented. And there wasn't any. So we don't know this. We just don't know. So that's the issue here. And that's where the trial court, I think, based this decision saying it would be mere speculation. And that's what we would let the jury do if we allowed the case to proceed to a jury trial. They wouldn't hear any evidence.

speaker: bethmyers
text: You have about one minute left.

speaker: johnbenintendi
text: Okay. So they wouldn't have that evidence that would allow a proper inference. We don't allow a proper inference based upon conjecture, speculation. It has to be evidence provided. And that's been the whole issue in this case. Negligence cannot be presumed. It must be proven. That's Katzenzano versus Kroger from the First District Court of Appeals. It must be proven. And it has not been proven in this case.

speaker: bethmyers
text: Thank you. Mr. Valentin, you have five minutes remaining. You are on mute. So we'll ask you to start over.

speaker: koryveletean
text: There we go. Ms. Hayden told me to make sure I muted it when I wasn't speaking. So I apologize. With all due respect to Mr. Benedetti in this court, I do believe it's completely illogical for the appellant to be required to measure this puddle of water to figure out how deep it was on a ceramic tile floor or to somehow test the temperature to figure out if it was hot or if it was cold.

speaker: bethmyers
text: Well, let me ask a question though. That may be true. I mean, you have the obligation to prove it and you can do it in a lot of different ways. But for example, wouldn't it be possible to get an expert to testify as to what kind of a drip there was and at what velocity it was dripping so that a juror could make a reasonable inference about how long it had been there?

speaker: koryveletean
text: Well, a couple of things would prevent that, I believe, Your Honor. I believe one, how probative would that testimony be in light of the store manager's testimony? He specifically said that it was not actively leaking at the time of his inspection after the incident. So our expert would have had, I think he would not have been able to go back in and somehow recreate the speed in which the water was leaking onto the ground. There was a trail, it was coming directly from the freezer. The cause of the water going on the ground was the defective door seals. Judge Winkler brought up an issue about any ongoing problems with the door freezers. Judge Winkler, this was kind of a funny portion of the store manager's testimony, his deposition testimony, because he denied there being any ongoing problems. Denied not having knowledge of any issues with the door freezers. And then completely blew his mind when I showed him photographs that were attached and utilized as exhibits that shows problems that spanned all the way down the aisleway after the incident. So this wasn't just a merely one isolated type of an event. And I believe Judge Brock, that could go back to rebut any foundation to the employee in creating the defective door seals. Because there is record evidence after the fact that shows that there were issues all the way down this freezer. It just shows that what happens in these slip and fall cases, again, it's a catch 22 issue. You either have to identify the source or hazard, then identify the source, and then come up with the defendants having knowledge of it. But what do they do? What have they done in this particular case? Denied, denied, denied, denied, denied. We did not know anything about it. You can't establish that we had knowledge. You can't establish constructive knowledge. Well, we do have physical evidence and videotape. It was produced in discovery, but for the convenience of the defendant, what was produced? The moments before the appellant's fall. It doesn't show the 30 minutes or half hour or an hour or two hours before the incident and shows what they could have in terms of inspected. It didn't show the entire day. Okay, you do have to, there's only so much record evidence that you can establish when the store managers deny having any ongoing knowledge of any problem. Say that they do inspections, but there's no records of it. And that's clear in the record testimony that they didn't do any type of inspection. They didn't do any type of cleaning. They hired a third party in, but there was record testimony that the last time that there was clean was I believe 24 hours before. So you don't have anyone going up and down the aisles and creating any type of logs in terms of inspections. You just have denied, denied, denied, denied. I do nothing about it. Thank you.
